title: Ancient Trees in Italy: Cities to Explore
meta_description: Italy's oldest trees hide behind walls: villa gardens, cloisters, a botanical garden Goethe wrote about in 1786. 28 cities mapped, 320 trees.
intro: Padua's botanical garden opened in 1545 and one of its founding plants is still alive: a dwarf fan palm that Goethe wrote an entire essay about in 1786, using it to illustrate his theory of how plants grow. That tree sets Italy's pattern. Its oldest survivors stand less in open woodland than behind walls someone built on purpose, villa gardens, monastery cloisters, university botanical collections kept for study rather than shade. Rome's own oldest confirmed tree, a 425-year-old oriental plane, grows in a garden laid out for a cardinal. Italy's national tree register lists more monumental specimens than any other country mapped here, but carries no age field at all, so most of the dates on this site come from regional catalogues and city archives instead, the same close reading that first put a number on Goethe's palm.
